items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to find the shortest distance between the point [MATH: P(3,0,-2)] and the plane [MATH: \Pi] that is given by the equation [MATH: (\mathbf{r}-\langle 2 , 3 , 1 \rangle ) \cdot \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle = 0.]

Content:
First, note that [MATH: \mathbf{n} = \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle] is a vector that's normal to the plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/29bc6fded08b250d82443fe75c3b5e30]

Content:
Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, [MATH: Q(2,3,1)]. Then

Content:
[MATH: PQ^(→)|= ⟨2, 3, 1⟩ − ⟨3, 0, − 2⟩; = ⟨ − 1, 3, 3⟩.]

Content:
The shortest distance [MATH: d] from the point [MATH: P] to the plane [MATH: \Pi] is the absolute value of the scalar projection of [MATH: \overrightarrow{PQ}] onto the normal vector of the plane, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d1672d9ff9800e86987f2f2f955f82d5]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: d|=|comp_{n}PQ^(→)|; = (|PQ^(→) ⋅ n|)/(|n|); = (|(− 1) ⋅ 4 + 3 ⋅ 4 + 3 ⋅ 2|)/(sqrt(4^{2} + 4^{2} + 2^{2})); = (|− 4 + 12 + 6|)/(sqrt(16 + 16 + 4)); = (|14|)/(sqrt(36)); = (7)/(3).]

Content:
We conclude that the shortest distance from the point [MATH: P] to the plane [MATH: \Pi] is [MATH: \dfrac{7}{3}.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, [MATH: Q(4,8,2).] Then

[MATH: PQ^(→)|= [4; 8; 2] − [5; 2; − 2] = [− 1; 6; 4].]

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector [MATH: [2; 4; − 4]]

Finally, the shortest distance from the point [MATH: P] to the plane [MATH: \Pi] is the absolute value of the scalar projection of [MATH: \overrightarrow{PQ}] onto the normal vector of the plane:

[MATH: d|=|comp_{n}PQ^(→)|; = (|PQ^(→) ⋅ n|)/(|n|); = (|(− 1) ⋅ 2 + 6 ⋅ 4 + 4 ⋅ (− 4)|)/(sqrt(2^{2} + 4^{2} + (− 4)^{2})); = (|− 2 + 24 − 16|)/(sqrt(4 + 16 + 16)); = (|6|)/(sqrt(36)); = 1]

sections.normalized_html: Find the shortest distance between the point [MATH: P(3 , -10 , 3)] and the plane [MATH: \Pi] with equation [MATH: 2x+y-2z = -1].
sections.readable_text: Find the shortest distance between the point [MATH: P(3 , -10 , 3)] and the plane [MATH: \Pi] with equation [MATH: 2x+y-2z = -1].

sections.normalized_html:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] into the equation and solve for [MATH: z.] Let's choose [MATH: x=4] and [MATH: y=-5] (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for [MATH: z,] we get

[MATH: 2x + y − 2z|= − 1; 2(4) + (− 5) + 1|= 2z; 4|= 2z; z|= 2.]

So, we get the point [MATH: Q(4, -5, 2)] which lies on the plane.

Computing [MATH: \overrightarrow{PQ},] we get

[MATH: PQ^(→)|= ⟨4, − 5, 2⟩ − ⟨3, − 10, 3⟩; = ⟨1, 5, − 1⟩.]

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane [MATH: ax+by+cz=d,] the normal vector is [MATH: \mathbf{n}=\langle a,b,c \rangle.] So, for the plane [MATH: \Pi,] we have [MATH: \mathbf{n}= \langle 2, 1, -2 \rangle.]

Finally, the shortest distance from the point [MATH: P] to the plane [MATH: \Pi] is the absolute value of the scalar projection of [MATH: \overrightarrow{PQ}] onto the normal vector of the plane:

[MATH: d|=|comp_{n}PQ^(→)|; = (|PQ^(→) ⋅ n|)/(|n|); = (|1 ⋅ 2 + 5 ⋅ 1 + (− 1) ⋅ (− 2)|)/(sqrt(2^{2} + 1^{2} + (− 2)^{2})); = (|2 + 5 + 2|)/(sqrt(4 + 1 + 4)); = (|9|)/(sqrt(9)); = 3]
